mcqs.question: Which layer assignment correctly matches the data type to the cache layer?
options: Static assets belong in the app-layer cache since it's the fastest layer to reach
Static assets → CDN/client; shared computed results → app-layer cache; per-row lookups → DB layer
Every data type should go through the CDN since it sits closest to the user
The database layer should be skipped entirely once an app-layer cache is in place
mcqs.explanation: Each layer fits a different access pattern: the CDN is best for static, shared bytes; the app layer is best for shared computed results; the DB layer's own cache is best for repeated row reads. Routing static assets through the app layer or everything through the CDN ignores that mismatch, and the DB layer still matters for data the app-layer cache doesn't hold.

mcqs.question: On the same page load, where should a per-user session token and the site's static logo each be cached?
options: Cache both at the CDN, since they're both requested on every page load
Cache both in the app-layer distributed cache, since it's the more secure option
Cache the session token at the app layer (per-user, not shared) and the logo at the CDN (identical for everyone)
Cache the session token at the CDN with a very short TTL and the logo at the app layer
mcqs.explanation: The session token is per-user data that must never be shared across users, so it belongs at the app layer, keyed per user. The logo is identical for every request, so it belongs at the CDN where it can be served to everyone from the edge. Putting the token at the CDN risks leaking it toward another user; putting the logo at the app layer wastes distributed-cache capacity on something that never varies.

mcqs.question: With four cache layers stacked (client, CDN, app, DB), how do you find out which one served a particular stale response?
options: Tag each response with which cache layer served it, so a stale report can be traced back to the exact hop
Assume the database is always correct, so staleness can only come from the app layer
Restart every cache layer whenever a user reports stale data
Increase every layer's TTL so staleness reports happen less often
mcqs.explanation: Tagging the response (a cache-status header or log field per hop) is the only way to actually localize which layer served the stale copy — otherwise you're manually checking dev tools, CDN dashboards, and cache TTLs one at a time. The staleness can originate at any layer, not just the app layer; restarting caches is destructive and doesn't diagnose anything; and raising TTLs makes staleness worse, not less frequent to investigate.

mcqs.question: What's the real problem with putting every kind of cached data — sessions, static config, computed prices, rate-limit counters — into one shared Redis cluster?
options: It's fine as long as the cluster has enough total memory for all the workloads combined
It ignores that static assets belong at the CDN, and mixes unrelated access patterns onto one cluster's eviction policy, so one workload's churn can evict another's hot keys
Redis cannot technically store more than one data type in the same cluster
It's wrong because Redis clusters can't be scaled horizontally
mcqs.explanation: The real risk is contention over the eviction policy and capacity: a bursty, high-churn workload (like rate-limit counters) can evict genuinely hot keys from a calmer workload sharing the same cluster, and none of this data should include static assets, which belong at the CDN regardless of memory headroom. Redis supports mixed data types fine, and it does scale horizontally — neither is the actual problem.
